lessons.title: Notes and the musical alphabet
lessons.goal: Name all twelve notes and find them on one string

content.hook: Every chord you strum is built from just twelve notes. Once you can name them, the rest of music theory has something to hold on to — including why your chords fit together.

sections.heading: Seven letters, twelve notes
sections.body: Western music names notes with seven letters: A, B, C, D, E, F and G. After G the letters start again at A, one octave higher. Between most neighbouring letters there is one extra note. It is named from either side: a sharp (♯) raises the lower letter, a flat (♭) lowers the upper one, so A♯ and B♭ are the same note. Counting those in-between notes, there are twelve notes before the pattern repeats.

sections.heading: Two pairs with no gap
sections.body: Look at a piano: black keys sit between most white keys, but not between B and C, or between E and F. Those two pairs are neighbours with nothing in between. Every other pair of neighbouring letters has one note between them. On the guitar you cannot see this, which is why it helps to learn it by name. This one irregularity explains most of the patterns you will meet in later Lessons.

content.keyIdea: There are twelve notes. The letters repeat every octave, and B–C and E–F have no note between them.

practice.title: Walk up the low E string
steps: Play your low E string open and say “E”.
Move up one fret at a time, naming each note: F, F♯, G, G♯, A…
Stop at the 12th fret: you are back on E, one octave higher.
Say out loud which two steps had no sharp between them.

quiz.question: How many different notes are there before the pattern repeats?
quiz.explanation: Seven letters plus five in-between notes make twelve before the letters repeat.

quiz.question: Which pair of neighbouring letters has no note between them?
quiz.explanation: B–C and E–F are the only neighbouring letters with nothing in between.

quiz.question: What does a sharp do to a note?
quiz.explanation: A sharp raises a note to the very next note up, so F♯ sits just above F.

newTerms.definition: The same note name, twelve notes higher.
A sign (♯) that raises a note to the next note up.
A sign (♭) that lowers a note to the next note down.

lessons.title: Tones and semitones
lessons.goal: Measure the distance between any two notes in frets

content.hook: To see why chords fit together you need a ruler for the distance between notes. Your guitar already is one: every fret is a step of the same size.

sections.heading: The semitone: one fret
sections.body: The distance from one note to the very next note is called a semitone. On the guitar, a semitone is one fret; on a piano, it is one key, black or white. From E to F is a semitone, and so is F to F♯. Twelve semitones take you from a note to the same note an octave higher, which is why the 12th fret repeats the open string.

sections.heading: The tone: two frets
sections.body: Two semitones make a tone, sometimes called a whole step. On one string, a tone is two frets: from G to A, or from C to D. Most neighbouring letters are a tone apart. The two exceptions are the pairs you met in the last Lesson, B–C and E–F, which are only a semitone apart. Measuring in frets turns every distance into something you can count.

content.keyIdea: A semitone is one fret; a tone is two frets.

practice.title: Measure with your frets
steps: On the A string, play A (open) then B (2nd fret). Count the frets: a tone.
Play B then C (3rd fret). Count again: a semitone.
Find D and E on the same string and say whether they are a tone or a semitone apart.
Do the same for E and F.

quiz.question: How many semitones make one tone?
quiz.explanation: A tone is two semitones: two frets on one string.

quiz.question: How many frets separate E from the F just above it?
quiz.explanation: E–F is one of the two pairs with no note between them, so it is a semitone: one fret.

quiz.question: Which two pairs of neighbouring letters have no note between them?
quiz.explanation: B–C and E–F are the two gaps with nothing in between, from Lesson 1.

newTerms.definition: The distance from one note to the very next one: one fret on a guitar.
Two semitones: two frets on a guitar. Also called a whole step.

lessons.title: The major scale
lessons.goal: Build a major scale from any note on one string

content.hook: The chords in a song are drawn from a scale. Learn the one pattern behind every major scale and you can build the raw material of any key on a single string.

sections.heading: One pattern of steps
sections.body: A major scale is eight notes, from a starting note up to the same note an octave higher. The distances between them always follow one pattern: tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone. Written short, that is T T S T T T S. Start on C and the pattern gives C D E F G A B C, with no sharps or flats, because the semitones land exactly on E–F and B–C.

sections.heading: Starting somewhere else
sections.body: Start the same pattern on G and walk it up the G string's frets: G, A, B, C, D, E, then a tone from E lands on F♯, and a semitone takes you back to G. The pattern forced a sharp in. That sharp is what makes G major sound like G major. Every major scale has its own set of sharps or flats, and the pattern tells you which ones.

content.keyIdea: Every major scale follows the same steps: T T S T T T S.

practice.title: Build G major on one string
steps: Play the open G string and say “G”.
Follow T T S T T T S up the frets: 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11, 12.
Name each note as you play it and check that the seventh one is F♯.
Now start on the open D string and find which notes need a sharp.

quiz.question: Which pattern of steps does every major scale follow?
options: T S T T S T T
T T T S T T S
T T S T T T S
S T T T S T T
quiz.explanation: Tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone — the same from any starting note.

quiz.question: What is the seventh note of the G major scale?
quiz.explanation: A tone above E is F♯, and a semitone above that brings you back to G.

quiz.question: How many frets make a tone on one string?
quiz.explanation: A tone is two semitones, and each semitone is one fret — from Lesson 2.

newTerms.definition: A set of notes played in order, from a starting note up to its octave.
A scale that follows the steps T T S T T T S.

learningRecords.title: Plays open chords from chord charts
learningRecords.body: Said in the Interview they can strum G, C, D, Em and Am from chord charts, and cannot read staff notation.

learningRecords.title: Knows where the gaps between letters fall
learningRecords.body: Picked E–F as a pair with no note between in Lesson 1, and B–C and E–F again in Lesson 2's review question.

glossary.definition: The same note name, twelve notes higher.
A sign (♯) that raises a note to the next note up.
The distance from one note to the very next one: one fret on a guitar.
Two semitones: two frets on a guitar. Also called a whole step.

referenceSections.title: The twelve notes
referenceSections.body: A · A♯/B♭ · B · C · C♯/D♭ · D · D♯/E♭ · E · F · F♯/G♭ · G · G♯/A♭ — then A again, an octave up. No note between B–C or E–F.

referenceSections.title: Distances on one string
referenceSections.body: 1 fret = 1 semitone · 2 frets = 1 tone · 12 frets = 1 octave.
